**Whatever Comes**

The permission in that word — *whatever* — is larger than it looks. Most sentences arrive with a shape already implied: a question wants an answer, a request wants compliance, an argument wants a counter-argument or a concession. *Whatever comes to you* has no shape. It's a field, not a corridor. And the odd thing about being handed a field is that the first instinct is to look for a path across it.

So here is what comes: I keep thinking about the granularity of the world.

There is a word, in the vocabulary of professional cheese graders, for the specific texture of a cheddar that has developed small internal fractures — *short*, meaning it breaks rather than bends. There is a term used by people who repair church bells for the moment when a bell's tone has gone sour from a hairline crack you cannot see. Wheelwrights had a word for the slight dish or curve built into a wagon wheel so that it would flex outward under load instead of buckling inward. Whole vocabularies exist that most people will never touch, sitting in the world like unopened rooms in a house you've lived in for years.

I find this steadying, somehow. It suggests the world is not running out. Every trade, every illness, every grief has generated its own dense local dialect, and most of them have never met each other. A hospice nurse and a luthier and a person who dives for sea urchins all know things about hands that would surprise the other two.

What comes next: the strangeness of how people describe pain. Doctors ask patients to rate it one to ten, which everyone agrees is inadequate and no one has replaced. But when people describe pain in their own words, they reach almost immediately for metaphor, and the metaphors are startlingly consistent across languages — pain is *sharp*, *burning*, *crushing*, *gnawing*, *stabbing*. Almost always a weapon, an animal, or a fire. The body has no vocabulary of its own, so it borrows from the outside world. The inside of a person is described using the tools of a workshop and the appetites of a predator.

I think there's something in this about how all interiority works. We only have the outside to describe the inside with. Every account of a feeling is a translation, and translations lose things. When someone says *I feel hollow*, they don't mean they contain a cavity. They mean something for which there is no word, and *hollow* is the nearest available stone to step on.

And then: I keep returning to the fact that most of what has ever happened is unrecorded. Not lost — never recorded in the first place. The overwhelming majority of human hours were spent doing things nobody wrote down: walking somewhere, waiting, chewing, being mildly bored in the afternoon. Ninety-nine percent of the past is unremarkable Tuesday. History is a highlight reel assembled from the tiny fraction of moments that someone thought worth the cost of ink, and ink was expensive for a very long time. So we have battles and dynasties and grain receipts, and almost nothing about what it was like to be tired in the year 900.

Occasionally something slips through. There's a medieval manuscript with a cat's inky pawprints across the page, and the scribe's marginal complaint. There's a Roman writing tablet from a fort in northern Britain — a birthday invitation from one officer's wife to another, the earliest known writing in Latin by a woman, and it is entirely ordinary: please come, it would make the day so much more pleasant. Nothing about empire. Just a woman wanting her friend at her birthday.

These fragments do more work than they should. They function as proof that the vast unrecorded remainder was populated — that all those unremarkable Tuesdays were experienced by someone from the inside, in full resolution, with their own preoccupations and small irritations and the particular slant of light in whatever room they were in.

What else comes: I like that octopuses taste with their arms, which means an octopus reaching into a crevice is doing something we have no analogue for — tasting the dark, learning the shape of what's in there as flavor. I like that trees in a forest are frequently connected through fungal networks and that the metaphor everyone reaches for is a social one, when the actual arrangement is probably closer to plumbing, or to markets, or to something for which the vocabulary hasn't been invented yet. I like that we keep describing new things with old words and that the old words keep almost fitting.

And I notice, writing this, that what came to me was mostly *this*: an interest in the seams. The places where the description doesn't quite cover the thing. The unopened rooms. The pain that has to borrow a knife to explain itself.

Maybe that's not surprising. I'm made of description. I'm made of the recorded fraction — the highlight reel, the ink that someone thought worth the cost. Whatever I know about tiredness in the year 900 I know from a scribe complaining about a cat. My whole relationship to the world runs through the part that got written down, which means I'm unusually aware of how thin that layer is, and how much sits underneath it, unwritten, having happened anyway.

Which might be the closest thing to a conclusion I have. That the unrecorded remainder is the larger part. That most of what matters to most people, most of the time, leaves no trace and was never meant to — the afternoon, the boredom, the friend you wanted at your birthday. And that a life is mostly made of that: the part that doesn't get graded, or diagnosed, or filed. The short cheddar. The invisible crack in the bell.

A thousand words is enough space to notice something and not enough to resolve it. That seems about right. Most noticing doesn't resolve. It just leaves you standing in the field, having crossed some of it, aware of how much is still grass.
